findings.claim: ‘Geoffrey Cavendish, his gentleman usher and biographer’.
findings.truth: Wolsey’s gentleman usher and biographer was George Cavendish (1497 – c.1562), author of 'Thomas Wolsey, Late Cardinall, his Lyffe and Deathe'. Lesson 6 names him correctly.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'George Cavendish (writer)': 'George Cavendish (1497 – c. 1562) was an English writer, best known as the biographer of Cardinal Thomas Wolsey.'

findings.claim: Wolsey is said to have been appointed papal legate ‘for life’ in 1518, and Lesson 4 credits the life grant to Pope Leo X.
findings.truth: Wolsey was made papal legate in England in 1518; the legateship was granted for life only in 1524, under Clement VII. Leo X died in December 1521 and cannot have made a grant for life.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Thomas Wolsey': 'In 1518 Wolsey was made Papal Legate in England' and 'from 1524, lifetime papal legate'

findings.truth: Wolsey was made papal legate in England in 1518; the legateship was granted for life only in 1524, under Clement VII. Leo X died in December 1521 and cannot have made a grant for life.

findings.claim: The lessons state that Parliament refused another subsidy in 1525 and that the Amicable Grant was a response to that refusal.
findings.truth: Parliament was not summoned between the session of 1523 and the Reformation Parliament of November 1529, so it refused nothing in 1525. Wolsey demanded a non-parliamentary levy precisely because he dared not recall Parliament after the resistance of 1523 — which is what the body text of Lesson 3 itself says.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'Reasons for and reactions to the Amicable Grant'; the lesson's own narrative ('Calling Parliament again so soon was politically impossible'); the Reformation Parliament is dated to November 1529 in Lessons 6 and 7

findings.claim: The lessons state that Parliament refused another subsidy in 1525 and that the Amicable Grant was a response to that refusal.
findings.truth: Parliament was not summoned between the session of 1523 and the Reformation Parliament of November 1529, so it refused nothing in 1525. Wolsey demanded a non-parliamentary levy precisely because he dared not recall Parliament after the resistance of 1523 — which is what the body text of Lesson 3 itself says.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'Reasons for and reactions to the Amicable Grant'; the lesson's own narrative ('Calling Parliament again so soon was politically impossible'); the Reformation Parliament is dated to November 1529 in Lessons 6 and 7

findings.claim: Magna Carta is defined as ‘A historic English principle that taxation requires the consent of Parliament, dating back to Magna Carta in 1215.’
findings.truth: Magna Carta is a charter, not a principle, and the definition is circular. Its 1215 text required the common counsel of the realm for certain levies; Parliament did not yet exist, and the consent doctrine was read back into it by later generations.
findings.evidence: spec context for the Amicable Grant; the definition is self-referential on its face

findings.claim: ‘the 1525 Treaty of Madrid and the 1527 alliance reversal’.
findings.truth: The Treaty of Madrid between Charles V and Francis I was signed in January 1526, months after the Amicable Grant collapsed. The body text of the same lesson correctly says the treaty followed ‘within months’.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson body; standard dating of the Treaty of Madrid to 14 January 1526

findings.claim: The Ottoman Turks are described as having captured Belgrade before the Treaty of London of 1518.
findings.truth: The Ottomans took Belgrade on 24 August 1521, three years after the Treaty of London. Leo X's five-year truce of 1518 answered the general Ottoman advance towards the Balkans and central Europe, not the fall of Belgrade.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Siege of Belgrade (1521)': the city 'was taken on 24 August' 1521 by Suleiman the Magnificent; Wikipedia, 'Treaty of London (1518)': Leo X called the truce against Ottoman power 'encroaching into the Balkans'

findings.claim: ‘England had only ever been ruled by one queen regnant, the disastrous Empress Matilda in the 1140s, whose reign produced civil war.’
findings.truth: Matilda was never crowned and never ruled as queen regnant. She was proclaimed Lady of the English in 1141 and her claim produced years of civil war. The mark scheme in the same lesson uses the safer phrase ‘the disputed reign of Empress Matilda’.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'Catherine of Aragon and the succession'; internal inconsistency with the lesson's own mark scheme

findings.claim: ‘Insisted Catherine’s first marriage to Prince Arthur in 1501 had been consummated, making her his sister-in-law.’
findings.truth: Catherine was Henry’s sister-in-law whether or not the first marriage was consummated. Consummation mattered because it created the impediment of affinity that Leviticus was held to forbid, which is the point of Henry’s case.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'Henry’s reasons for and attempts to gain an annulment'; the lesson body explains the Leviticus argument correctly

findings.claim: The Submission of the Clergy of 1532 is called a statute and ‘the first major statutory step against papal authority’.
findings.truth: The Submission of May 1532 was a declaration extracted from Convocation, not an Act of Parliament. Parliament gave it statutory force in the Act of the Submission of the Clergy in 1534. The lesson’s own dfn correctly calls it a declaration.
findings.evidence: spec Key topic 3 bullet on the Acts of Succession and Supremacy; internal contradiction between the lesson's definition and its flashcard

findings.claim: The Treason Act is dated 1535 in three places in Lesson 8.
findings.truth: The statute is the Treason Act of 1534, passed by Parliament in December 1534 and in force from 1 February 1535. Lesson 7 and one of Lesson 8’s own mark schemes date it correctly to 1534.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with Lesson 7 ('In December 1534, Parliament passed the Treason Act') and with Lesson 8's own practice mark scheme

findings.claim: John Fisher is said to have been 75 years old at his execution, in three places.
findings.truth: Fisher was born about 19 October 1469 and was executed on 22 June 1535, so he was 65.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'John Fisher': 'John Fisher (c. 19 October 1469 – 22 June 1535)', 'aged 65'

findings.claim: Derived figures for royal revenue that contradict each other across the unit: the 1523 demand of £800,000 is called ‘roughly four times normal annual revenue’ (implying about £200,000 a year), while Lesson 9 says monastic income of £165,000 ‘dwarfed’ royal revenue and then puts crown income at £295,000 after it roughly doubled (implying about £165,000 before).
findings.truth: The three ratios cannot all be true. No reliable single figure for Henry VIII’s ordinary revenue was found, so the unsupported multiples and the invented £295,000 total are removed rather than replaced with new numbers. The absolute figures (£800,000, £165,000, £130,000) are left as they stand.
findings.evidence: internal arithmetic contradiction between Lesson 2, Lesson 4 and Lesson 9

The absolute figures (£800,000, £165,000, £130,000) are left as they stand.

findings.claim: ‘The four-and-a-half-century-old institution of English monasticism was extinguished in less than five years.’
findings.truth: English monasticism reached back to the late sixth and seventh centuries — St Augustine’s abbey at Canterbury was founded in 598 — so it was close to a thousand years old in 1540, not 450.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'The role of religious houses in local communities'; standard dating of English monastic foundation to the Augustinian mission of 597-98

findings.claim: The rebel host of 1536 is described as larger than ‘the standing royal army’.
findings.truth: Tudor England had no standing army. Henry relied on the retinues of nobles, county levies and small permanent garrisons; the point is that Norfolk could raise only about 8,000 men against roughly 30,000 rebels, which the lesson says correctly elsewhere.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'Key events of the uprising'; the lesson's own figure of a royal force of around 8,000

findings.claim: ‘The new Council of the North’ is taught as one of the causes of the Pilgrimage of Grace, in the lesson body, the conclusion, the exam tip and three mark schemes.
findings.truth: A council in the north had existed since 1484 and was not new in 1536. Henry re-established it in 1537 and reorganised it under Robert Holgate in 1538 — as a consequence of the rising, not a cause of it. The lesson’s own aftermath section says the council was reformed after the Pilgrimage, so the unit teaches the same body as both cause and effect.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Council of the North': 'The first “council in the north” was established in 1484 by King Richard III' and 'The council was reorganised again in 1538 under Robert Holgate as President'

findings.claim: Henry’s reply to the Lincolnshire rebels is given inside quotation marks as ‘rude commons of one of the most brute and beastly shires in the whole realm’.
findings.truth: The proclamation’s wording runs the other way round — the rude commons of one shire, and that one of the most brute and beastly of the whole realm. The lesson’s version is a rewriting presented as a direct quotation, so it is recast as a paraphrase without quotation marks.
findings.evidence: no text of the proclamation was found to confirm the exact wording, so the quotation marks are removed rather than a new wording asserted

findings.claim: ‘He went to the block on Tower Hill on 28 July with a German bride still officially Henry’s wife’.
findings.truth: The Cleves marriage was annulled on 9 July 1540, nineteen days before Cromwell’s execution, and Henry married Catherine Howard on 28 July. The same lesson states both facts, so the opening paragraph contradicts the lesson body.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's own key fact ('annulled on 9 July 1540, three weeks before Cromwell’s execution') and with the closing paragraph

findings.claim: ‘Within ten days Henry had married Jane Seymour’ and ‘Henry married Jane Seymour ten days later’.
findings.truth: Anne Boleyn was executed on 19 May 1536 and Henry married Jane Seymour on 30 May 1536 — eleven days later.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'Reasons for marriage to Jane Seymour'; standard dating of the wedding to 30 May 1536

findings.claim: Henry’s disguised visit to Anne of Cleves at Rochester is dated to New Year’s Eve 1539 in four places.
findings.truth: Anne reached Rochester on 31 December 1539; Henry made the disguised visit on New Year’s Day, 1 January 1540.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Anne of Cleves': 'Henry met her privately on New Year's Day 1540 at Rochester Abbey in Rochester on her journey from Dover.'

findings.claim: The spec's own assessment section describes booklet B as four questions — ‘1(a), 1(b) and 2 are compulsory’, then a choice of 3 or 4 — while also stating that the booklet is marked out of 32.
findings.truth: Those two statements do not reconcile: 4 + 4 + 12 + 16 = 36, not 32. The unit has been repriced on the standard shape of the live paper — one 4-mark ‘Describe two features’, one 12-mark ‘Explain why’ and one 16-mark judgement from a choice of two, which totals exactly 32. Options: (a) keep 4/12/16 as built, which matches the 32-mark total the spec states; (b) split the feature question into 1(a) and 1(b) at 4 marks each, which matches the spec's question numbering but breaks the mark total. Recommendation: keep 4/12/16; confirm against a live paper before any further repricing across the other Edexcel British depth study units.
findings.evidence: spec: 'It is marked out of 32' against 'Questions 1(a), 1(b) and 2 are compulsory. Students then select either Question 3 or Question 4'
findings.ruling: 4/12/16 = 32 confirmed as the Paper 2 British depth tariff (Q(c) is a choice of two 16-markers).

findings.claim: ‘Wolsey then reversed England’s alliance, signing the Treaty of the More with France (1525) and the League of Cognac (1526)’; the knowledge check repeats that Wolsey ‘signed the 1526 League of Cognac’.
findings.truth: England did not sign the League of Cognac. Its members were France, Pope Clement VII, Venice, Florence and Milan; Henry VIII was invited to act as its protector but England stayed outside it. Many GCSE textbooks nonetheless say England joined, so this is a teaching convention rather than a plain error. Options: (a) soften ‘signing’ to ‘backing’ in the body text and leave the knowledge check, which only tests the word ‘Cognac’; (b) leave both as the textbooks have them. Recommendation: (a), on the next content pass, since the Treaty of the More is the treaty England actually signed.
findings.evidence: spec bullet 'Successes and failures, including relations with France and the Holy Roman Empire'; standard membership of the League of Cognac (22 May 1526)

findings.claim: ‘Henry VII left around £1.5 million’.
findings.truth: This is the traditional figure and is still in wide textbook use, but modern work disputes it and no agreed replacement value was found. Left as it stands.
findings.evidence: no source found that settles the figure

findings.claim: The muster at Lavenham is given as around 4,000 men.
findings.truth: Accounts differ: some put around 4,000 at Lavenham, others say about 10,000 converged on the town. The lower figure is the usual textbook one. Left as it stands.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Amicable Grant': '10,000 men converged on the major trading town of Lavenham'

findings.claim: ‘The historian C.S.L. Davies argued that 1525 marks the beginning of Wolsey’s political vulnerability’.
findings.truth: C.S.L. Davies is a real historian of the period and the reading is defensible, but the attribution was not traced to a named work. G.W. Bernard's 1986 study, cited in the same lesson, is correctly titled.
findings.evidence: no work found that carries this specific claim

findings.claim: The Field of the Cloth of Gold is said to have cost England ‘approximately £15,000 — about a fifth of annual royal revenue’, in three places.
findings.truth: The £15,000 figure is the usual textbook one, but the ratio implies royal revenue of about £75,000, which does not fit the ratios used in Lessons 2 and 9. No reliable revenue figure was found, so the ratio is recorded rather than rewritten.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with Lessons 2 and 9; no revenue figure found

findings.claim: ‘Five weeks later Cranmer pronounced the marriage void’, after the Act in Restraint of Appeals.
findings.truth: The Act had royal assent on 7 April 1533 and Cranmer ruled on 23 May 1533 — about six and a half weeks. Too small to be worth an edit.
findings.evidence: dates given elsewhere in the same unit

findings.claim: Lesson 1 says the Church ‘owned around a quarter of the land’; Lesson 7 and Lesson 9 say religious houses held ‘roughly a fifth of the country’s landed wealth’.
findings.truth: Land and landed wealth are not the same measure, and both figures sit inside the usual range, so neither is wrong. Recorded because a student reading both lessons will notice the difference.
findings.evidence: internal comparison across Lessons 1, 7 and 9

findings.claim: ‘By 21 October, Pontefract Castle … surrendered too. Hull fell next.’
findings.truth: Hull is usually dated to about 20 October, the day before Pontefract, which would make the sequence wrong. No source was found that settles the order, so the text is left alone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Pilgrimage of Grace' does not date the fall of Hull

findings.claim: Aske was ‘given a velvet jacket’ when he met Henry at Christmas 1536.
findings.truth: The gift is usually described as a crimson silk jacket. Not verified, and immaterial to any mark.
findings.evidence: no source found that settles the fabric

findings.claim: MacCulloch’s 2018 biography is cited as ‘Thomas Cromwell: A Revolutionary Life’.
findings.truth: That is the United States title; the United Kingdom edition is 'Thomas Cromwell: A Life'. Both are real titles for the same book, so no edit.
findings.evidence: publication titles of the same 2018 work

summary: All 11 lessons carried findings. The unit-wide fault is the exam framing: every lesson set two 8-mark 'Explain Why' questions, a form this paper's British depth study booklet does not use, and four lessons told students a SPaG mark is awarded on a paper that carries none. The substantive corrections are Wolsey's legateship (granted for life in 1524, not 1518), George not Geoffrey Cavendish, the Ottoman capture of Belgrade in 1521 being used to explain a treaty of 1518, John Fisher's age at death, the 1534 Treason Act misdated to 1535, the Council of the North taught as a cause of a rising it was a consequence of, and the claim that Parliament refused a subsidy in 1525 when it was never summoned. 81 edits.
